title: split-execution-kv-sharding-prototype-notes
content:
Purpose:
This note records an experimental prototype that splits inference execution across two kernel backends: a Triton/TensorRT path for dense transformer ops and a small custom CUDA kernel set for KV-cache management and selective attention ops. The goal is to explore tradeoffs when sharding KV state across GPUs and doing per-request kernel selection. These are rough notes: design, configs, microbench results, and next steps.

Background and motivation:
- Problem: Large context LLMs push KV cache memory beyond a single GPU and introduce non-trivial token-by-token overhead from KV read/writes.
- Hypothesis: Keeping dense matmuls in high-performance vendor runtimes (Triton/TF-TRT) while moving compact, latency-sensitive KV ops to hand-optimized CUDA kernels can reduce end-to-end p99 and reduce memory pressure via fine-grained sharding.
- Additional opportunity: Allow runtime to pick a per-request execution plan based on seq_len, batch_shape, and per-model shardability annotation.

High-level design:
- Execution split: encoder/decoder dense layers executed by Triton served TensorRT engines (via Triton backend). KV-cache read/write and small attention pre/post-processing executed via custom CUDA kernels loaded by the serving runtime as a separate adapter.
- KV sharding: logical KV space sharded with consistent hashing across N GPUs. Each GPU stores local shards for keys/values. For multi-GPU requests, we try to colocate microbatches to minimize cross-GPU fetches.
- Routing: request header contains preferred_shard_hint (computed by router from user session); fallback policies: local_approximate_fetch -> rendezvous gather -> CPU fallback.
- Kernel handshake: Triton engine is given placeholder buffers for KV lookups. At runtime the adapter populates those buffers using CUDA IPC or peer-to-peer DMA where available.

Prototype setup and configs:
- Hardware: 4x A100 40GB in a single node with NVLink, PCIe fallback enabled.
- Software: Triton 23.09, TensorRT 9.4, CUDA 12.2. Runtime branch: feature/split-kv-shard-proto.
- Model: Llama-2-13B distilled-ish graph compiled to TRT engines with attention split points annotated.
- KV layout: (num_heads=64, head_dim=128) stored as float16; per-token KV size ~ 16KB for seq_len=8192.
- Sharding strategy tried: (1) contiguous chunking, (2) consistent-hash by session_id.

Key experiments and observations:
1) Microbatch colocate vs scatter-gather:
  - Colocate microbatching (assign whole request to primary shard) minimized cross-GPU traffic but increased tail latency when primary shard overloaded.
  - Scatter-gather (split tokens across shards) reduced p50 but increased p99 due to synchronization waits.
2) CUDA Graph warmup for KV kernels:
  - Capturing repeated KV read patterns into CUDA Graphs reduced kernel-launch overhead by ~18% on steady traffic. Warmup cost is non-trivial for first few requests; need warmup heuristics.
3) Peer-to-peer DMA vs CUDA IPC:
  - NVLink-enabled P2P copies were ~2.5x faster than staging via host pinned memory. When NVLink disabled, overhead killed p99. Runtime should detect topology and choose staging strategy per-request.
4) Memory fragmentation from mixed runtimes:
  - TensorRT allocation behavior caused fragmentation when large TRT engines coexisted with many small CUDA allocations for KV. Observed usable GPU memory drop by ~9% compared to single-runtime baseline.
5) Fallbacks and graceful degradation:
  - When a shard runs out of memory, CPU fallback for KV reads increased token latency by 6–8x but kept throughput. Useful as emergency mode.
6) Quantization and precision mismatch:
  - Dense engines run FP16 in TRT; custom KV kernels also used FP16, but occasional sub-token numerical drift seen on -O3 compress paths. Recommend per-model eval to set tolerance.

Metrics (approx):
- Baseline (all-triton): avg latency 74ms, p95 190ms, p99 320ms, GPU mem usage 38GB per GPU.
- Split-proto (colocate shards): avg latency 66ms, p95 172ms, p99 275ms, GPU mem usage 33.5GB effective (after accounting for KV shards).
- Split-proto (scatter-gather): avg latency 62ms, p95 160ms, p99 390ms (p99 regress due to sync), GPU mem 34.2GB.
Notes: results vary strongly with request mix and seq_len distribution.

Operational concerns:
- Complexity: introducing two runtime paths increases BLAM surface area (bugs, metrics to correlate). Suggest adding per-request trace ids that include plan chosen.
- Monitoring: must expose KV-shard-hit metrics, cross-GPU bytes, per-shard queue length, and kernel invocation latencies.
- Autoscaling: shard-aware autoscaling needed so we can scale capacity by shard; naive pod autoscaler can create imbalance.
- Security: CUDA IPC and P2P require careful privileges in multi-tenant setups; not feasible for hosted customers without isolation.

Open design questions / TODOs:
- Warmup strategy: how many CUDA graphs to keep per model/seq_len bucket before eviction? Could use LRU with hit-count thresholds.
- Shard placement policy: simple consistent-hash vs learning-based placement based on access pattern?
- Per-request planner: heuristics table vs small learned policy; needs safety net for oscillation.
- Fallback latency budgeting: how long to wait for rendezvous gather before CPU fallback?
- Memory accounting: can we request soft-reservation from Triton engines to reduce fragmentation?

Short term next steps (2–4 weeks):
- Instrument end-to-end traces for a larger traffic mix (including short-chat vs long-context).
- Implement a topology-aware transfer policy: prefer NVLink, else staged pinned host copies.
- Add warmup agent that pre-captures CUDA Graphs for top-k request shapes.
- Run quantization sensitivity tests on eval prompts to catch drift.

Medium term (quarter):
- Integrate planner into router with simulated replay experiments.
- Prototype shard-aware autoscaling and cost model for dedicated fleet.
- Harden security model for CUDA IPC and produce a private-deploy only path.

Appendix: rough commands used for running experiments:
- tritonserver --model-repository=/tmp/trt_models --backend-config=tensorrt,profile=defer
- ./runtime_worker --backend-adapter=/opt/adapters/kv-adapter.so --shard-config=cons_hash:4
- perf capture: nvprof --metrics gld_throughput,gst_throughput ./test_client --scenario=longcontext

Quick conclusions:
- Split execution shows promise for memory-limited setups and can decrease average latency, but scheduling and synchronization choices strongly affect p99.
- NVLink topology is a gating factor; without fast interconnect split-exec often regresses.
- Operational complexity is non-trivial; recommend feature-flagged prototypes for Dedicated/Private customers first.

Unresolved: precise safety thresholds for automatic fallback and a canonical per-model tolerance for mixed-precision drift.

Notes-to-self: link to benchmark scripts and raw perf CSVs in the linked artifacts. Need to summarize into a follow-up PR with automated replay and perf plots for the eng review doc.
